metadata.title: Big Tech Earnings Face a $600 Billion Question: Is AI Spending Paying Off?

content.text:
Artificial intelligence helped lift U.S. stocks Monday, but this week's earnings from Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon will test whether enthusiasm for the technology can survive closer scrutiny of its enormous cost.
The three companies, which have nearly $1.7 trillion in combined backlog, plan to spend as much as $600 billion this year. Investors now want evidence that customers are adopting their AI services quickly enough to support that infrastructure buildout without squeezing margins and free cash flow.
"I want to hear who's paying for AI and whether they're spending more," Scott Martin, CIMA partner at Kingsview Wealth Management, tells First for Money. "Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon can announce enormous investments, but shareholders need some sense of how those investments turn into revenue and, eventually, cash."
Alphabet and Microsoft report Wednesday, followed by Amazon on Thursday. Analysts expect all three companies to post accelerating cloud growth, making their results a key measure of AI demand and its economic viability.
Google Cloud revenue is expected to surge 95.1% to $29.57 billion for the September quarter, up from 81.8% growth in the previous quarter, according to LSEG data. Amazon Web Services revenue is projected to rise 38.2%, while Microsoft Azure is expected to grow 47.7%, according to Visible Alpha.
"For everyday investors, I'd focus on three things: cloud growth, profit margins and cash flow after spending on infrastructure," Martin says. "If demand is strong, are customers actually using more services? Is the company making money on that business? And how much more does it need to spend to keep growing?"
Cash generation could become particularly important. Alphabet and Amazon are expected to burn cash for their second and third consecutive quarters, respectively, while Microsoft is projected to generate more than $8 billion in cash flow.
Meta already demonstrated how demanding investors have become. Better-than-expected revenue growth and an upbeat outlook were eclipsed by higher spending plans, sending its shares down nearly 7% the following day. Meta has since announced plans to raise as much as $95 billion in equity to help fund AI-related expansion.
ZUMAPRESS.com / MEGA
Concerns about borrowing costs and debt-funded infrastructure have intensified as higher U.S. interest rates loom. Still, Anthropic's initial public offering filing helped revive optimism Monday, contributing to a 0.70% gain for the S&P 500 and a 0.83% rise for the Nasdaq.
